title: Calculus I–II
subject: Calculus
summary: A complete single-variable calculus course built for physics: limits, derivatives, integrals, techniques, series and Taylor expansion, and a first look at differential equations. Emphasis on approximation, integration technique fluency, and the chemistry-flavoured uses (rate laws, Arrhenius, gas work, harmonic approximation).

units.title: Limits and Continuity
units.summary: The limit as the core idea of calculus: one- and two-sided limits, limit laws, the squeeze theorem, continuity, and the epsilon-delta definition; the same 'close enough' reasoning behind every physical idealisation (point mass, instantaneous rate).

lessons.title: Limits: the idea, numerically and graphically
objectives: Explain, in words and with a secant-to-tangent picture, how the slope of a secant line becomes the slope of a tangent line as the interval shrinks to zero.
Estimate a limit from a table of values and from a graph, and say when a limit does not exist (jump, blow-up, oscillation).
Evaluate one-sided limits and state that a two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree.
Evaluate limits at which the function is undefined by algebraic simplification (factor-and-cancel, rationalise, common denominator).

lectures.title: Limits and the definition of derivatives

lessons.title: Limit laws, the squeeze theorem, and continuity
objectives: Apply the limit laws (sum, product, quotient, power) and know the conditions under which each holds.
Use the squeeze theorem to prove lim_{x->0} sin x / x = 1 and lim (1 - cos x)/x = 0, and state why these limits matter for the derivatives of the trig functions.
State the three-part definition of continuity at a point and classify removable, jump and infinite discontinuities.
State the intermediate value theorem and use it to show that an equation has a root in an interval.

lessons.title: The precise definition of a limit
objectives: State the epsilon-delta definition of lim_{x->a} f(x) = L as a logical statement with quantifiers.
Given epsilon, find a valid delta for a linear function and for x^2 near a point, and explain what 'delta may depend on epsilon' means.
Write a short epsilon-delta proof for a limit of a linear function.
Negate the definition to say what it means for a limit not to equal L.

units.title: Derivatives
units.summary: The derivative as limit and as function; all the differentiation rules, implicit differentiation, derivatives of inverse, exponential and log functions, and rates of change including related rates.

lessons.title: The derivative: definition, interpretation, and as a function
objectives: Write the derivative as a limit of difference quotients and compute it from the definition for polynomials, 1/x and sqrt(x).
Interpret f'(a) as the slope of the tangent line, the instantaneous rate of change, and, given units, as a physical quantity (e.g. velocity, reaction rate d[A]/dt).
Write the equation of the tangent line to y = f(x) at x = a.
Sketch the graph of f' from the graph of f and vice versa.
Explain the relationship between differentiability and continuity, with the example f(x) = |x| at 0.

lessons.title: Differentiation rules: power, sum, product, quotient
objectives: Derive the power rule for integer exponents and apply it for rational exponents.
Differentiate with the constant multiple, sum, product and quotient rules and explain why (fg)' is not f'g'.
Differentiate the same expression two ways (e.g. rewriting a quotient as a product) and confirm that the answers agree.
Compute higher derivatives and interpret the second derivative as acceleration or curvature.

lessons.title: Derivatives of trigonometric functions and the chain rule
objectives: Derive d/dx sin x = cos x and d/dx cos x = -sin x from the definition using the two basic limits.
Differentiate tan, sec, csc, cot using the quotient rule.
State the chain rule in Leibniz form and apply it to nested compositions, e.g. d/dx sin(x^2), d/dx (3x+1)^7.
Differentiate x(t) = A cos(omega t + phi) twice and show that it satisfies x'' = -omega^2 x.

lessons.title: Implicit differentiation and derivatives of inverse, exponential, and logarithmic functions

State the formula (f^{-1})'(b) = 1/f'(a) and use it to derive the derivatives of arcsin, arccos, and arctan.
Show d/dx e^x = e^x, d/dx ln x = 1/x, and d/dx b^x = b^x ln b.
Use logarithmic differentiation to differentiate f(x)^{g(x)} and long products or quotients.
Differentiate k = A exp(-Ea/RT) with respect to T and interpret the result as the temperature sensitivity of a rate constant.

units.title: Applications of Derivatives
units.summary: Linear and quadratic approximation, differentials, the mean value theorem, extrema and curve sketching, optimisation, limits at infinity, L'Hopital's rule and Newton's method; approximation is the physicist's main use of the derivative.

lessons.title: Linear approximation, differentials, and quadratic approximation
objectives: Write the linearisation L(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a) and use it to estimate values such as sqrt(4.1) and (1.02)^10.
Compute the differential dy = f'(x) dx and use it to estimate propagated error and relative error in a measured quantity (e.g. volume from a measured radius).
Derive the second-order approximation f(a) + f'(a)h + f''(a)h^2/2 and compare it with the linear one for e^x, sin x, and (1+x)^p.
Justify the physics approximations sin x ~ x, (1 + x)^n ~ 1 + n x, and e^x ~ 1 + x near zero, with the error estimate.
Treat df = f'(x)dx as the first-order change of a quantity such as PV or E(T), the idea behind exact differentials later in thermodynamics.

State the mean value theorem and Rolle's theorem and use them to show that f' = 0 implies f is constant.
Determine intervals of concavity and inflection points from the sign of f'', and relate them to the shape of a potential-energy curve (stable and unstable equilibria).
Sketch a function using intercepts, asymptotes, f', and f'' as a coordinated analysis.

Set up an optimisation problem: define the objective, the constraint, the domain, and check the endpoints.

lessons.title: L'Hopital's rule and Newton's method
objectives: Recognise indeterminate forms 0/0, infinity/infinity, 0*infinity, infinity - infinity, 1^infinity, and 0^0 and rewrite them for L'Hopital's rule.
Apply L'Hopital's rule correctly, checking its hypotheses, and compare growth rates of exponentials, powers and logarithms.
Derive Newton's method x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n) from the tangent line and apply two or three iterations by hand.
Explain when Newton's method fails or converges slowly, and use it to solve a transcendental equation (e.g. a Wien's law condition or an equilibrium expression).

units.title: Integration
units.summary: Antiderivatives, Riemann sums, the definite integral, both parts of the fundamental theorem, substitution, integrals of exponentials and inverse trigonometric forms, and applications to area, volume, average value and work.

objectives: Find antiderivatives of polynomials, trig, and exponential functions, and verify them by differentiation, including the arbitrary constant.
Solve a simple initial value problem v(t) = a t + v0 for position (kinematics from constant acceleration).
Approximate an area by left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums with n rectangles and see how the error depends on n.
Write a Riemann sum in sigma notation and take the limit as n -> infinity to define the integral.

State both parts of the fundamental theorem of calculus and explain why differentiation and integration are inverse operations.
Evaluate definite integrals by finding an antiderivative and computing F(b) - F(a).
Differentiate a function defined as an integral, d/dx of the integral from a to g(x) of f(t) dt, using the chain rule.

units.title: Techniques of Integration
units.summary: Integration by parts, trigonometric integrals and substitution, partial fractions, strategy, and improper integrals and numerical integration; the toolkit for evaluating the integrals that appear in quantum and statistical mechanics.

Evaluate definite integrals by parts, including the boundary term uv evaluated at the limits.

Integrate tan^m x sec^n x by the appropriate identity and substitution.

Complete the square to bring a quadratic under a radical to standard form, as needed for hydrogen-atom and Coulomb-field integrals.

Apply the trapezoid and Simpson's rules and describe how their errors scale with step size.
Evaluate integral x^n e^(-x) dx = n! and relate it to the gamma function and to hydrogen radial-wavefunction normalisation.

units.title: Sequences and Infinite Series
units.summary: Sequences, infinite series, and the standard tests for convergence; the foundation of power series and every perturbative expansion that follows.

lessons.title: Sequences, infinite series, and the divergence and integral tests
objectives: Determine whether a sequence converges and compute its limit, using monotone-and-bounded reasoning where needed.
Define the sum of an infinite series as the limit of partial sums and sum geometric and telescoping series.
Apply the divergence test (nth-term test) and the integral test, and state what each does and does not prove.
State and use the p-series result, and explain why the harmonic series diverges although its terms go to zero.

lessons.title: Comparison, alternating, ratio, and root tests
objectives: Apply the comparison and limit comparison tests with a suitable benchmark series.
Apply the alternating series test and bound the truncation error by the first omitted term.
Apply the ratio and root tests, particularly to factorial and exponential terms, and recognise when they are inconclusive.
Distinguish absolute from conditional convergence and state why rearranging a conditionally convergent series can change the sum.
Choose a test for a given series and justify the choice in one or two sentences.

units.title: Power Series and Taylor Series
units.summary: Power series, radius of convergence, Taylor and Maclaurin series, error bounds, and the standard expansions; heavily used in physics, from the pendulum and relativistic kinetic energy to the harmonic approximation of molecular potentials.

lessons.title: Power series and their calculus
objectives: Find the radius and interval of convergence of a power series using the ratio test and check the endpoints.
Differentiate and integrate a power series term by term within its radius of convergence.
Obtain new series from the geometric series by substitution, differentiation and integration (e.g. series for 1/(1+x^2), arctan x, ln(1+x)).
Add, multiply, and divide power series to a given order.
demoIdeas: Radius-of-convergence viewer: partial sums of a chosen series plotted against the function, with the interval of convergence shaded.

lessons.title: Taylor and Maclaurin series
objectives: Derive the Taylor series coefficients c_n = f^(n)(a)/n! by matching derivatives at a point.
Write from memory the Maclaurin series for e^x, sin x, cos x, 1/(1-x), ln(1+x), and (1+x)^p, with their intervals of convergence.
Construct Taylor polynomials of a given degree about a point other than 0.
Show that Euler's formula e^(ix) = cos x + i sin x follows from the series for e^x, sin x, and cos x.
Interpret the n-th Taylor polynomial as the best degree-n polynomial approximation near the expansion point.
demoIdeas: Taylor builder: add terms one at a time to sin x, e^x, ln(1+x) and watch the polynomial hug the curve; show where it fails outside the radius.

lessons.title: Working with Taylor series: error bounds and physics approximations
objectives: Bound the error of a Taylor polynomial using Taylor's remainder theorem and the alternating-series estimate.
Evaluate limits and integrals by expanding in series (e.g. (sin x - x)/x^3, integral of sin(x^2)).
Expand the relativistic energy E = mc^2 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) to get mc^2 + mv^2/2, and a pendulum or Morse potential about its minimum to get the harmonic approximation.
Expand a molecular potential V(r) about its minimum r_e to second order to identify the force constant k = V''(r_e) and the vibrational frequency.
Choose the expansion variable and order for a given physical regime (small x versus large x) and state the validity condition.
demoIdeas: Anharmonic well: overlay a Morse potential and its harmonic Taylor approximation and show where the approximation breaks down as energy rises.

units.title: A First Look at Differential Equations
units.summary: Separable and first-order linear ODEs, exponential growth and decay, and the logistic equation, enough for kinetics and for the full ODE course (M4).

lessons.title: Separable and first-order linear differential equations

Solve separable equations dy/dx = g(x)h(y) by separating variables and integrating, and solve exponential growth and decay.
Solve a first-order linear equation y' + p(x)y = q(x) with an integrating factor.
Solve the first-order and second-order integrated rate laws and a Newton cooling equation, and state the half-life dependence on initial concentration for each order.
Read a direction field and sketch solution curves; describe the logistic equation's equilibria and stability.
